headline: GAO Flags 11 Priority Recommendations Still Open at GSA
dek: The watchdog says real-property planning, shared-service data and federal-award oversight could unlock tens of millions in savings and improve controls over hundreds of millions in annual spending.

sources.title: Priority Open Recommendations: General Services Administration

lead.creator: Ajay Suresh
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic, verified by Wikimedia Commons Flickr review.
lead.attribution: Ajay Suresh / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
lead.caption: The General Services Administration headquarters in Washington in 2024. GAO identified 11 priority recommendations still open at the agency in June 2026.
lead.alt: Front of the General Services Administration headquarters building in Washington, D.C.

charts.caption: GSA had 38 open GAO recommendations in June 2026, including 11 designated as priorities.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 38 open GAO recommendations at GSA, including 11 priority recommendations.

charts.caption: GAO grouped its priority concerns around real property, shared services and federal-award oversight.
charts.alt: Graphic lists federal real property, shared services and federal awards as three priority areas.

paragraphs: The Government Accountability Office identified 11 priority recommendations still open at the General Services Administration as of June, concentrating its concerns on federal buildings, government-wide shared services and federal-award oversight.

GSA had 38 open GAO recommendations in total. The watchdog classifies a recommendation as a priority when implementation could significantly improve operations, generate large savings, reduce mismanagement or advance a high-risk issue.

The agency's overall implementation record was strong: GAO reported that GSA had implemented 97% of recommendations made five years earlier. Since a May 2025 priority letter, GSA implemented two priority recommendations, lost the priority designation on one and received six new priority items.

On real property, GAO said a 2025 Public Buildings Service reorganization included significant workforce reductions but did not fully follow selected reform practices. It called for a plan to identify and close skill gaps.

GAO also said GSA's approach to speeding disposal of underused buildings lacked clear performance goals. The watchdog estimated that better workforce and disposal planning could produce tens of millions of dollars in savings over 10 years.

For shared services such as financial management and human resources, GAO found that GSA lacked comprehensive performance data. It recommended a plan and timeline for collecting measures, including cost data, that could support tens of millions in potential savings over three years.

The third area is the Federal Audit Clearinghouse. GAO found accuracy, consistency and completeness problems in award data reported by recipients and recommended more training for recipients and auditors.

GAO said better clearinghouse data could help resolve audit findings associated with hundreds of millions of dollars in federal spending each year. That figure describes spending linked to findings, not an estimate of fraud or guaranteed recoveries.

The priority letter does not establish that every recommendation will yield its maximum estimated benefit. The measurable follow-up is whether GSA closes the 11 items with documented workforce plans, disposal goals, shared-service measures and improved audit data.
facts: GSA had 38 open GAO recommendations as of June 2026.
Eleven were designated priority recommendations.
GSA's five-year recommendation implementation rate was 97%.
GAO highlighted real property, shared services and federal-award oversight.
Two priority recommendations had been implemented since GAO's May 2025 letter.
uncertainty: GAO's potential savings figures are estimates, not realized benefits.
The hundreds of millions tied to audit findings is not an estimate of fraud or recoverable losses.
seoTitle: GAO flags 11 priority recommendations still open at GSA
seoDescription: GAO says GSA has 11 priority recommendations open across federal property, shared services and award oversight.

headline: Federal Robbery Sentences Averaged 108 Months in Fiscal 2025
dek: The Sentencing Commission counted 1,233 robbery cases; sentences averaged 160 months with a Section 924(c) conviction and 72 months without one.

lead.creator: Carol M. Highsmith
lead.rightsBasis: Public-domain dedication by the photographer; Library of Congress reports no known restrictions on publication.
lead.attribution: Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress
lead.caption: The Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse in Milwaukee in 2021. New Sentencing Commission data describes 1,233 federal robbery cases in fiscal 2025.
lead.alt: Historic stone federal building and United States courthouse in Milwaukee.

charts.caption: Robbery accounted for 1,233 of the 66,662 federal cases reported for fiscal 2025 and declined 4% from fiscal 2021.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 1,233 robbery cases, 66,662 total cases and a 4 percent decline since fiscal 2021.

charts.caption: Average sentences were 160 months with a Section 924(c) conviction and 72 months without one.
charts.alt: Graphic compares average sentences of 160 months with Section 924(c) and 72 months without it.

paragraphs: Federal robbery sentences averaged 108 months in fiscal 2025, according to a new United States Sentencing Commission profile of 1,233 cases.
Robbery cases represented 1.8% of the 66,662 federal cases reported for the year. The number was 4% lower than in fiscal 2021, and the category covers cases sentenced under the robbery guideline.

A conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), which carries a consecutive punishment for using or carrying a firearm in specified circumstances, sharply changed the average. The mean was 160 months with a Section 924(c) conviction and 72 months without one.

Forty-one percent of people sentenced for robbery also had Section 924(c) convictions. Overall, 99% received prison sentences and 42% were convicted of an offense carrying a mandatory minimum penalty.
The Commission reported a median loss of $2,400. Seventy-seven percent of cases involved losses of $20,000 or less, while 11% involved losses above $95,000.

Guideline adjustments describe recurring case features. Sixty-two percent involved use or brandishing of a firearm or dangerous weapon, or a threat of death; 21% involved carjacking; 19% involved abduction or physical restraint; and 17% involved bodily injury.

The five districts with the most robbery cases were the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, Northern District of Illinois, Southern District of New York, Southern District of Texas and Southern District of Florida.
The data reports sentencing outcomes after conviction, not arrests, pending accusations or local robbery rates. It should not be used to infer guilt or conduct in any unresolved case.

Averages also compress wide differences in statutes, guideline calculations and judicial decisions. The Commission's strongest comparison is the documented split between cases with and without Section 924(c), not a prediction of an individual sentence.
facts: USSC reported 1,233 federal robbery cases in fiscal 2025.
The average sentence was 108 months.
Average sentences were 160 months with Section 924(c) and 72 months without it.
Forty-one percent also had Section 924(c) convictions.
Ninety-nine percent received prison sentences.
uncertainty: The figures summarize sentenced federal cases and do not measure arrests, pending cases or local crime rates.
Category averages do not predict an individual sentence.
seoTitle: Federal robbery sentences averaged 108 months in FY2025
seoDescription: USSC counted 1,233 federal robbery cases in fiscal 2025, with average sentences of 160 months with Section 924(c) and 72 without.

headline: Library of Congress Trained 90 Educators to Teach With Primary Sources
dek: The three summer institutes selected participants from nearly 200 applicants across 21 states and the District of Columbia.

sources.title: Ninety Teachers Participate in National Education Initiative at Library of Congress

lead.creator: Awinebotima
lead.caption: A teacher-training workshop in 2024. The Library of Congress says its 2026 summer institutes trained 90 educators to use primary sources in classrooms.
lead.alt: Educators seated in rows during a teacher-training workshop.

charts.caption: The Library selected 90 educators from nearly 200 applicants for its 2026 summer institutes.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 90 selected educators from nearly 200 applicants.

charts.caption: Participants represented 21 states and the District of Columbia across three three-day institutes.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 21 states, the District of Columbia and three teacher institutes.

paragraphs: The Library of Congress trained 90 educators to use primary sources in classrooms through its 2026 Summer Teacher Institute, selecting them from a pool of nearly 200 applicants.
Participants represented 21 states and the District of Columbia. The Library held three institutes in Washington, each organized as a three-day program.

The institutes are part of the Teaching with Primary Sources program. Library education specialists and subject experts worked with participants on methods for examining historical artifacts and documents.
The practical aim is classroom transfer: educators develop primary-source teaching strategies they can use in their own districts and share with colleagues.

The Library describes primary-source analysis as a way to prompt questions, critical thinking and evidence-based knowledge construction. The institutes exposed participants to millions of digitized items available through loc.gov.
The cohort extended beyond classroom teachers. It included school library media specialists, administrators, public librarians and educators working across K-16 settings.
The participating institutions ranged from large metropolitan systems to smaller rural districts. The public list included schools and libraries from Alabama to Washington and Wisconsin.
The release documents reach and selection, not an evaluation of student outcomes. It does not report a control group, classroom achievement measures or a long-term follow-up of teachers.

The next evidence of impact will be whether participants publish or share lesson materials, train colleagues and document how students use the Library's primary sources after returning to their communities.
facts: Ninety educators participated in the 2026 institutes.
They were selected from nearly 200 applicants.
Participants represented 21 states and the District of Columbia.
The Library offered three institutes, each lasting three days.
The program included classroom teachers, librarians, administrators and other K-16 educators.
uncertainty: The Library's release does not measure student outcomes or long-term classroom effects.
Participation counts do not show how broadly materials will be reused after the institutes.
seoTitle: Library of Congress trained 90 teachers on primary sources
seoDescription: The Library of Congress selected 90 educators from nearly 200 applicants for three 2026 primary-source teaching institutes.

headline: CBO Says the 2026 Defense Request Reached $961 Billion
dek: The request included $113 billion from the 2025 reconciliation law, and CBO says the funding mix makes enduring costs harder to project.

sources.title: DoD's 2026 Budget Request and Plan for Funding Provided by the 2025 Reconciliation Act

lead.creator: U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Brittany A. Chase
lead.rightsBasis: Public-domain work of a U.S. Department of Defense employee created as part of official duties.
lead.attribution: U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Brittany A. Chase / Department of Defense
lead.caption: An aerial view of the Pentagon in 2021. CBO says the 2026 defense request totaled $961 billion, including reconciliation funding.
lead.alt: Aerial view of the Pentagon and its surrounding roads and parking areas.

charts.caption: The $961 billion request included $113 billion from the 2025 reconciliation law.
charts.alt: Graphic lists a 961 billion dollar defense request including 113 billion dollars in reconciliation funding.

charts.caption: Acquisition funding totaled $384 billion; $89 billion of that was mandatory reconciliation funding.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 384 billion dollars for acquisition, including 89 billion dollars in reconciliation funding.

paragraphs: The Department of Defense's fiscal 2026 budget request totaled $961 billion, including $113 billion from the 2025 reconciliation law, according to a Congressional Budget Office analysis.
Adjusted for inflation, CBO called the request one of the three high-water marks in defense funding over the past 50 years, alongside requests for 1985 and 2010.
The comparison is not a measure of military activity. CBO focused on the base budget and enduring costs, excluding supplemental and emergency funding used for specific operations.

The missing planning document is central to the uncertainty. Defense did not release a 2026 Future Years Defense Program, so CBO based projections on the annual request, the 2025 plan and other official materials.
Acquisition funding totaled $384 billion, 18% more than the inflation-adjusted amount appropriated for 2025 and 21% more than Defense anticipated for 2026 in its prior five-year plan.

Mandatory reconciliation funding supplied $52 billion for procurement and $37 billion for research, development, testing and evaluation. Together those amounts were 79% of the $113 billion reconciliation placeholder in the request.

Base-budget acquisition funding was $295 billion, 9% below the inflation-adjusted 2025 appropriation and 7.4% below the prior plan. CBO said that pattern suggests reconciliation money was replacing some expected base resources, not only adding to them.

Operation and support totaled $558 billion, including $23 billion in reconciliation funding for operation and maintenance. The law's defense funding remains available through September 2029, unlike a typical one-year appropriation.

CBO treats the reconciliation amount as a one-year increment in its projection. If the higher level persists, future enduring costs would be higher; without a 2026 five-year plan, the report cannot determine whether the increase is temporary or permanent.
facts: The fiscal 2026 defense request totaled $961 billion.
It included $113 billion from the 2025 reconciliation law.
Acquisition funding totaled $384 billion.
Base-budget acquisition funding was $295 billion.
Operation and support funding totaled $558 billion.
uncertainty: CBO had no 2026 Future Years Defense Program and used other official planning records.
CBO treats reconciliation funding as a one-year increment; persistent funding would raise projected enduring costs.
seoDescription: CBO says the 2026 Defense request totaled $961 billion, including $113 billion in reconciliation funding that complicates long-term projections.

headline: Craig Tiley Begins USTA CEO Tenure After 21 Years at Tennis Australia
dek: The former Australian Open tournament director takes over as the U.S. association targets 35 million players by 2035 and prepares for the 2026 U.S. Open.

sources.title: Craig Tiley begins tenure as the USTA's chief executive officer

lead.creator: Kurt Kaiser
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal public-domain dedication.
lead.caption: Community tennis courts in Florida in 2020. Craig Tiley began his USTA chief executive tenure at the association's Orlando campus.
lead.alt: Several blue and green outdoor tennis courts viewed from above the surrounding fence.

charts.caption: Tiley joined the USTA after a 21-year career at Tennis Australia, where he led the Australian Open.
charts.alt: Graphic lists a 21-year Tennis Australia career and leadership of the Australian Open.

charts.caption: The USTA's stated participation goal is 35 million U.S. tennis players by 2035.
charts.alt: Graphic lists the USTA goal of 35 million tennis players by 2035.

paragraphs: Craig Tiley has begun work as chief executive of the United States Tennis Association, moving from a 21-year career at Tennis Australia to lead the U.S. governing body and the U.S. Open.

Tiley most recently served as Tennis Australia's chief executive and Australian Open tournament director. The USTA announced his appointment in February, and he started at the association's Orlando campus on July 20.
The leadership change comes as the USTA says U.S. tennis participation has grown for six consecutive years. Its long-range organizational goal is to reach 35 million players by 2035.

Tiley's portfolio combines community participation, player development, coaching, leagues and stewardship of the U.S. Open. Those responsibilities make the role broader than tournament operations alone.
The 2026 U.S. Open begins with Fan Week on Aug. 23 and main-draw play on Aug. 30, giving the new chief executive an immediate major-event test.

The association is also in the middle of a multiyear redevelopment at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center. Construction and event delivery will remain visible operating issues during his first seasons.

Tiley said his aim is to work across the tennis community to extend participation growth. USTA board chair Brian Vahaly highlighted his experience spanning college coaching, community tennis and Grand Slam administration.

The appointment announcement does not provide a new budget, participation projection or performance contract. Six years of reported growth does not by itself establish that the 35 million target will be reached.

The concrete measures of the transition will be participation counts, membership and coaching reach, player-development outcomes, U.S. Open delivery and whether the association publishes milestones toward its 2035 goal.
facts: Craig Tiley began as USTA chief executive on July 20, 2026.
He spent 21 years at Tennis Australia.
He most recently led Tennis Australia and the Australian Open.
The USTA reports six consecutive years of participation growth.
The association's stated goal is 35 million players by 2035.
uncertainty: The appointment release does not set interim milestones for the 35 million-player goal.
Future participation and event results depend on execution beyond the leadership announcement.
seoTitle: Craig Tiley begins tenure as USTA chief executive
seoDescription: Craig Tiley begins as USTA CEO after 21 years at Tennis Australia, with a 35 million-player goal and the 2026 U.S. Open ahead.

headline: NIH Expands All of Us Research Dataset to 747,000 Participants
dek: The ninth curated release links more than 535,000 whole genomes with nearly 482,000 electronic health records and adds proteomics, RNA and long-read sequencing.

sources.title: NIH's All of Us Research Program is now the largest integrated genomics and health database in the world

lead.creator: Linda Bartlett / National Cancer Institute
lead.rightsBasis: Public-domain work released without reuse restrictions by the creator and National Cancer Institute.
lead.caption: Scientists examine DNA-sequencing output in a National Cancer Institute laboratory. NIH's latest All of Us release includes more than 535,000 whole-genome sequences.
lead.alt: Two scientists in lab coats examine illuminated DNA sequence information in a laboratory.

charts.caption: CDRv9 includes data from 747,028 participants, more than 535,000 whole genomes and nearly 482,000 electronic health records.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 747,028 participants, more than 535,000 genomes and nearly 482,000 health records.

charts.caption: The release adds nearly 10,000 proteomics records, nearly 9,000 RNA-sequencing records and more than 14,500 long-read genomes.
charts.alt: Graphic lists proteomics, RNA sequencing and long-read genome counts in the new release.

paragraphs: The National Institutes of Health has expanded the All of Us Research Program's curated dataset to more than 747,000 participants, its largest data release to date.

The ninth curated repository includes more than 535,000 whole-genome sequences linked with nearly 482,000 electronic health records. NIH describes that combination as the world's largest integrated genomic and EHR database.
The controlled-tier characterization report gives an exact participant count of 747,028, an increase of 17.91% from the prior release's 633,547 participants.

The release also moves the program into multiomics. It includes proteomics data from nearly 10,000 participants, RNA-sequencing data from nearly 9,000 and long-read whole genomes from more than 14,500.
NIH reported more than 1.3 billion genetic variants, 553,000 genotyping arrays, 96,000 structural-variant records and 600,000 physical measurements in the broader release.

More than 645,000 people in the dataset, 86% of the total, come from communities NIH classifies as historically underrepresented in biomedical research. Participants span all 50 states and territories.
Registered researchers can use the cloud-based Researcher Workbench without a data-access fee, although computing and controlled-tier governance requirements still shape practical access.

Scale does not eliminate bias or missingness. The characterization report explicitly tells researchers to consider completeness, data sources and limits on generalizing findings to populations not represented in the same way.

The release is research infrastructure, not a clinical test or treatment. Its value will depend on reproducible studies, careful privacy controls and validation of discoveries in independent populations before clinical use.
facts: CDRv9 contains data from 747,028 participants.
It includes more than 535,000 whole-genome sequences.
Nearly 482,000 participants have linked electronic health records.
The participant count increased 17.91% from CDRv8.
The release adds proteomics, RNA sequencing and long-read genome data.
uncertainty: Large cohort size does not remove missingness, selection bias or limits on generalization.
The data release is research infrastructure and does not itself establish clinical utility.
seoTitle: NIH All of Us dataset reaches 747,000 participants
seoDescription: NIH's All of Us CDRv9 includes 747,028 participants, over 535,000 genomes and nearly 482,000 linked health records.
